what: Folding the pair table by the signed Frobenius group <pi, -1>
machine: the same host as the reach-versus-memory run
why_it_is_sound: The factor base is closed under pi and under negation, so the set of pair sums S is closed under both: pi(P+Q) = pi(P)+pi(Q) and -(P+Q) = (-P)+(-Q) are again sums of base points. A table answering 'is rest in S' therefore needs one key per orbit, not one per pair.
why_the_enumeration_is_complete: Walking i over one representative of each signed orbit and j over the whole base reaches every orbit of ordered pairs: given (P,Q), let g carry P to the representative R of its own orbit; then (R, gQ) lies in the same orbit and is enumerated. That holds whatever the stabilisers are, so there are no false negatives - only the factor two of redundancy that the unordered i <= j symmetry would remove.
the_canonical_key: The least rotation of the abscissa's coordinates in a normal basis. In a normal basis {beta, beta^2, beta^4, ...} the Frobenius is a one-bit cyclic rotation of the coordinate word, since (sum c_k beta^(2^k))^2 = sum c_k beta^(2^(k+1)). So the orbit of x is the set of rotations of its coordinates and the least rotation names it: one linear map (eight byte-table lookups) and n rotations, nothing squared and nothing reduced. Negation never moves the abscissa, since -(x,y) = (x,x+y), so the sign half of the fold is free either way.

what_it_buys.stored_pairs: 61.0x fewer at n = 61 (n, not 2n: the unordered symmetry is left unfolded)

what_it_costs.build: 116.7 s with the squaring chain, 56.4 s now, for the same 258632192 pairs.
what_it_costs.recovery: 0.037 ms, against 8.66 ms before the orbit tag and 12.88 ms before that. It is now 1.4% of a decomposition rather than the majority of it.
what_it_costs.the_degenerate_key: O is the sum of every +/- pair, so every orbit representative stores an entry under its key and a lookup there offers every orbit at once. 14.02 ms for the 88816 pairs it legitimately returns -- bounded, and the two membership tests it used to go quadratic through are now sorts.

the_honest_number: 168x faster per decomposed target at equal memory: 0.455 s against 0.0027 s. The fold alone, on the code as it stood, was 2.0x; the rest is four costs that only a base eight times wider makes visible.
what_is_binding_now: The probes, and nothing else: recovery is 1.4% of a decomposition. That matters more than the speedup, because it restores the lever the fold exists for. Before the orbit tag, widening the base bought nothing -- probes fell as 1/|F|^2 but the O(|F|) recovery rose to meet them, so sqrt(2) more base was 15.3 ms against 15.6 ms, a wash. Now a sqrt(2) widening should be worth about 1.9x again.
not_claimed: That the fold is worth 61x end to end; it is not, and the run above says so. That the 4 GiB widths were run end to end; they are the sizing law evaluated at that budget, and the timed pair is the 0.64/1.15 GiB one.

superseded_measurement.note: Four measurements preceded the one under 'measured', each fixing something real. (1) Canonical key as a chain of n-1 squarings: probe 1172 ns, 2.0x end to end. (2) The key as a rotation in a normal basis: probe 340 ns, 2.8x. (3) Recovery through an open-addressed index and a blocked scan: 12.88 -> 8.66 ms, 3.2x. (4) The search taking any witness rather than the sorted one: about eleven recoveries a decomposition down to about one, 27.8x. What remained was that recovery was still O(|F|), which cancelled the base-widening the fold exists for.

the_orbit_tag: A folded entry was built as canon(P_rep(r) + P_j), so a target whose key matches it satisfies g.target = P_rep(r) + P_j for some g in G, and therefore target = g^-1 P_rep(r) + g^-1 P_j with the first summand in the SAME signed orbit r -- orbits being what G preserves. So recovery walks the 2n points of orbit r, not the base: 122 against 177632. The tag is stored in the high half of the rest word, so it costs no memory at all; the rest keeps sixteen bits, which lets a probe through wrongly about one time in four thousand rather than one in 2^28, and a wrong admission now costs an orbit walk of microseconds instead of a scan of the base.
a_bug_the_tag_exposed: Folded tables had been bucketing on the canonical key's high bits, and a canonical key is a minimum over n rotations -- far below the middle of the range -- so the whole table piled into the first few buckets. The presence filter hid it, because a probe that misses never reaches a run, but every hit walked an enormous one. Folded tables now bucket on the hash the filter and the rest are already made of, which is flat. Probe 374 -> 285 ns, and it was worth far more than that on hits.

the_lever_is_connected_again.what_was_predicted: Before running it: with recovery at 1.4% of a decomposition, a sqrt(2) widening of the folded base should be worth about 1.9x, where before the orbit tag it was worth nothing (15.3 ms against 15.6 ms).

what_was_measured.speedup: 1.93x and 2.04x on two runs of the same configuration

the_lever_is_connected_again.verdict: 1.9x to 2.0x on two runs, against a prediction of about 1.9x, with recovery growing 0.037 -> 0.042/0.044 ms as sqrt(2) says it should. The hit rate reached 1.000: every one of 21779 and 22619 targets decomposed. Both runs are recorded because a thirty-second window at a millisecond-scale cost is a few thousand samples of a geometric variable, and this note has once already mistaken two points of that noise for a law. This is the test that matters -- not that the fold is fast, but that widening the base is worth something again.
